extracted.intended_audience: machine learning researchers and practitioners designing and analyzing federated learning algorithms and systems
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and theoretical/empirical criteria for designing, analyzing, and deploying federated learning (FL) algorithms—covering optimization, convergence, communication/computation trade-offs, personalization, and systems-level constraints for cross-device and cross-silo settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statelessness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices are likely to participate no more than once in the training of a given model, so stateless algorithms are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rules out direct application of stateful optimization algorithms like ADMM and stateful compression strategies that modify updates based on residual compression errors from previous rounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client sampling / small participants per round
rubrics_metrics.description: Total number of devices is huge, necessitating algorithms that only require a handful of clients to participate per round (client sampling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithms must operate when only a random subset M of clients participate each round; do not assume all clients are available. Analysis should account for intermittent participation and randomly sampled client sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composability with secure aggregation, differential privacy, and compression
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms should compose with other techniques like cryptographic secure aggregation protocols, differential privacy (DP), and model/update compression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressing algorithms in terms of primitives like “sum over selected clients” and “broadcast to selected clients” provides a valuable separation of concerns, but may exclude certain techniques (e.g. asynchronous updates) that are incompatible with those primitives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for primitives (sum/broadcast) to enable separation of concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Express optimization algorithms in terms of primitives like sum over selected clients and broadcast to selected clients to enable combination with other systems techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aids composability with DP and secure aggregation, but may rule out approaches that rely on other interaction patterns (e.g. async or residual-state compression).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local computation / reduced communication (Federated Averaging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Performing multiple local SGD steps and communicating less frequently (Federated Averaging / local SGD) addresses data locality and limited communication on mobile devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While this saves communication, it introduces optimization-theory challenges (divergence between local models) and trade-offs between number of local steps K and convergence; choose K and M carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence guarantees under formal assumptions (IID case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide theoretical convergence rates under standardized stochastic optimization assumptions (e.g., H-smoothness, bounded stochastic gradient variance σ^2) for the IID-data case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convergence should be framed as upper bounds on E[F(x_T)] − F(x^*); compare to baselines (minibatch SGD, single-device SGD) and report terms separating 'statistical' and 'optimization' contributions (e.g., σ/√(T K M) vs H/(T K)^2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison to natural baselines (mini-batch SGD and sequential SGD)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate federated algorithms relative to minibatch SGD (accelerated minibatch) and sequential (single-device) SGD baselines to identify which terms (statistical vs optimization) are optimal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these baselines to interpret whether federated methods match statistical optimality or optimization optimality, and to highlight gaps (e.g., inability to match accelerated mini-batch SGD).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wall-clock convergence and runtime-aware design
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess convergence in wall-clock time taking into account per-iteration cost from communication and local computation, not just number of iterations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices (M, K, compression, etc.) should be tuned to minimize wall-clock error vs time; e.g., increasing K reduces communication but may slow per-step progress in terms of total sequential SGD steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off tuning of number of local steps K
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose K to balance increased divergence between local models (hurting per-step error) against reduced communication and per-iteration wall-clock time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adaptive strategies (e.g., adaptive K based on training loss) can be used. The optimal K depends on relative costs of communication vs computation and on dataset size N, M, T.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of client set size M per round (scalability vs straggler risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting a larger set of clients per round improves convergence but increases vulnerability to slow/failed clients (tail delays).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include over-provisioning and accepting first M updates, time windows letting clients do as many updates as possible, fixing τ local updates with asynchronous updates, but asynchronous approaches may complicate DP/secure aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness to stragglers and computational heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms must handle unpredictable client slowdown or failure (stragglers) and heterogeneity in clients' compute capabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approaches: over-provisioning clients, time-windowed variable local steps Ki, asynchronous/lock-free updates; theoretical analysis of error convergence under these is an open challenge and impacts bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation weighting and global update rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of aggregation (e.g., weighted average by local dataset size vs simple average) affects convergence; the original FedAvg uses weights proportional to dataset sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For IID data weighted average reduces to simple average; unclear which aggregation yields fastest error convergence in practice—aggregation should be considered a design parameter to tune/justify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling non-IID data and modeling heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms should address diverse non-IID client data using assumptions like bounded inter-client gradient variance, bounded optimal objective difference, or bounded gradient dissimilarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include adding proximal terms (FedProx), control variates (SCAFFOLD), modified sampling, or algorithms with specific non-IID convergence analysis; state assumptions explicitly when proving convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit non-IID assumption disclosure (BCGV, BOGV, BGV, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: State the key non-IID assumptions used for analysis (e.g., bounded inter-client gradient variance, bounded optimal gradient variance, bounded gradient dissimilarity) and report which assumptions each convergence result relies on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use notation/tables to summarize which algorithms require which non-IID/convexity/auxiliary assumptions and present simplified convergence rates accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and costs of variance-reduction, momentum, and adaptive methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate techniques like control variates (SCAFFOLD), client/server momentum, local-adaptive methods (Adagrad), and server-level adaptive optimization to improve convergence/generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about per-round communication costs (e.g., local momentum may double per-round communication), and whether methods require state on clients or only server changes; analyzing acceleration benefits in FL is challenging and often open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decentralized and periodic decentralized variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider connections to decentralized optimization (PD-SGD, MATCHA) to reduce communication by leveraging network topology and periodic communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodic decentralized SGD can be adapted to local-update regimes and possibly improve performance via randomized client sampling or topology-aware mixing; provide convergence analysis under stated network/connectivity assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization, multi-task learning, and multi-model approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: When data is heterogeneous, consider multi-model approaches (per-client or per-group models), featurization, multi-task learning (e.g., MOCHA), local fine-tuning, and meta-learning (MAML/Reptile) for personalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different approaches have different system requirements: multi-task often requires stateful clients and full participation (suitable for cross-silo), whereas fine-tuning and featurization can work with stateless clients. Discuss trade-offs and practical constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics for personalized performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Define comprehensive metrics for measuring personalized performance—e.g., decide whether small improvements across all clients or large improvements for a subset is preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state personalization objectives and population-level metrics; this area lacks consensus and is highlighted as an open problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: When is a global FL-trained model preferable?
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze conditions under which a global federated model outperforms independently trained per-device models (depends on dataset sizes, degree of non-IIDness, partitioning type).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider multiple baselines (per-device hk, global hFL) and quantify expected improvement; account for vertical partitioning and record linkage challenges where feature sets differ across parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperparameter tuning cost and robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is expensive in FL due to limited device resources and long wall-clock training; FL adds more hyperparameters (aggregation rule, clients per round, local optimizer configs, compression).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design algorithms that are easy-to-tune or robust (same hyperparameters work across datasets), and investigate adaptive/self-tuning algorithms; explicitly account for limited HPO budget in evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: System-level constraints for model/architecture design
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapting neural architecture design and ML workflows (augmentation, feature engineering, model selection, debugging) to resource-constrained, decentralized datasets is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider compute, communication, and client heterogeneity constraints when proposing architectures and training workflows; few public datasets with auxiliary features exist, so benchmark suitability should be discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling bias from realistic client eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice, servers may not be able to sample uniformly—only devices meeting eligibility (charging, idle, free WiFi) are selected; client availability varies diurnally and by characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithms and analyses should account for non-uniform, changing sampling (e.g., semi-cyclic sampling) and the resulting objective mismatch or bias; consider convergence under such selection processes.
